newsitem.title: HUNGARY: E.Europe bourses mostly immune to hectic Wall St.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe bourses mostly immune to hectic Wall St.

text.p: Central European bourses traded mostly horizontally this week, neither benefiting nor suffering too much from hectic movements on Wall Street.
Budapest, Warsaw and Bratislava remained virtually unchanged, Ljubljana gained ground, Bucharest drifted higher after falls, while Prague touched lows and Zagreb was mixed following earlier losses.

The Central European Share Index (CESI) which, after its regular review reflects price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian stocks instead of 73 before, trimmed earlier losses and ended half percent lower.
BUDAPEST
The Hungarian bourse remained virtually unchanged through the week as sessions were overshadowed by heavy trade in the market's highest capitalised issue, oil firm MOL.
MOL was volatile this week, plunging five percent on Monday as a result of a privatisation agency decision to raise the amount of shares to be offered to domestic investors.
But on Wednesday it rallied eight percent after a pricing late on Tuesday in a six-times oversubscribed global offering at $16.25 and at 2,970 forints for domestic investors.

External factors such as the Dow's or the dollar's movements had less impact on the market, which looks forward to more earnings reports, as well as an upcoming share issue in pharmaceuticals maker Richter.
On Friday the BUX index closed at 5,944.46 points, down 40.71 from an all-time high set last Wednesday -- the last trading day in the previous week.
WARSAW
The Warsaw Stock Exchange fell this week but analysts said it was likely to extend its horizontal trend, which has lasted more than a month, until September general elections.

Analysts said the expected sideways drift between 16,000 and 17,000 was likely as large investors, although cautious about buying before the vote, would probably refrain from significant selling due to Poland's generally good economic outlook.
"In the second and third quarter a flat market is likely until the elections, though just before the polls speculative buying might begin," said Grzegorz Cimochowski of ING Baring.

Analysts said the planned late May sale of shares in Poland's largest commercial bank, Bank Handlowy, might weaken prices of currently listed banks, already suffering after showing unspectacular earnings in the first quarter of 1997.
PRAGUE

The Czech PX50 index took a beating through the week falling to a year low on Friday of 503.2. Dealers blamed the steady downtrend on the combination of poor first quarter company earnings, pessimism about macro-economic prospects and inadequate regulation of the capital markets.

The decline of the PX50 was driven by the three most heavily weighted shares: SPT Telecom CEZ and Komercni Banka. All three, which taken together account for 45 percent of the index's capitalisation, touched year lows during the week.
"It's anybody's guess but I wouldn't be so surprised to see them (the afore-mentioned shares) take the market down another 10-20 percent," said one local dealer.
BRATISLAVA

The Bratislava bourse continued stagnating due to low liquidity this week, but brokers said conditions in the neighbouring Czech Republic, where the market and crown are both losing value, could push investors to the Slovak market instead in the near future.
The official 16-share SAX index rose 0.74 points, or 0.38 percent, over the week to close at 194.54 on Friday.
"Though it is generally pretty quiet at the moment, I think investors will come back soon," Bohus Betko of ING Barings said. LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares jumped 3.45 percent this week as the blue-chips SBI index rose 45.39 points to 1,361.95 on Friday. Turnover tripled to 420.4 million tolars from 140.7 million.

Traders said moderate rise in prices was likely to continue for the next few weeks in expectation of fresh foreign buying, when the first custody accounts, which have to be opened by international portfolio investors under a central bank decision in February, are seen by mid-May.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks closed mixed after trading at lower levels in lacklustre activity throughout the week and traders said they expected interest to increase next week due to a correction in prices.

The most active stocks that could pull the market up, namely drugs firm Pliva, Zagrebacka Banka and food processor Podravka declined through the week and were not poised for growth although traders predicted they would stabilise.
BUCHAREST
The Bucharest bourse's first tier, which has been taking strong volumes since the start of the year, maintained command of the market this week.

But, with investors reluctant to pay higher prices for some of the high-caps, first-tier quotes drifted sideways on Thursday and three closed flat on Friday, holding to a resistance level. The second tier featured dull trading.
Two unofficial bourse indices, the VAB and the BIG, drifted higher on Friday by 2.5 and 2.45 percent, respectively, from the previous session.
